claim: The authors previously compared transcriptome data from hospitalized COVID-19 patients to control patients without COVID-19 and found changes in procoagulant and fibrinolytic gene expression in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.
source: Previously, we compared transcriptome data from hospitalized COVID-19 patients to control patients without COVID-19 and found changes in procoagulant and fibrinolytic gene expression in the lungs of COVID-19 patients (Mast et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Mast et al., 2021).

claim: The findings about changes in procoagulant and fibrinolytic gene expression were challenged based on issues with the samples, including library depth, library preparation, and control group meta-data.
source: These findings were subsequently challenged based on issues with the samples, including library depth, library preparation, and control group meta-data (FitzGerald and Jamieson, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the critical commentary (FitzGerald and Jamieson, 2022).

claim: The authors' revisited analyses of the two data sets are comparable to one another and support their original conclusions.
source: We have revisited our previous analyses of these two data sets, and we find that they are comparable to one another and support our conclusions.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reanalysis of their data, which is described in the manuscript.

claim: Most of the BALF samples in Michalovich et al. harbored comorbidities such as asthma, nicotine dependence, and obesity.
source: Most of the BALF samples in Michalovich et al. harbored comorbidities such as asthma, nicotine dependence, and obesity.

claim: Of the 40 control samples, three were reported to be free of comorbidities.
source: Of the 40 control samples, three were reported to be free of these comorbidities (putatively 'healthy').
evidence: The claim describes the composition of the control sample set.

claim: Michalovich et al. used a polyA enrichment method, which removes most ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
source: Michalovich et al. used a polyA enrichment method, which removes most ribosomal RNA (rRNA), and for the 9 cases, total RNA that includes rRNA was prepared.
evidence: The claim describes the library preparation method used in the Michalovich et al. study.

claim: For the 9 cases, total RNA that includes rRNA was prepared.
source: Michalovich et al. used a polyA enrichment method, which removes most ribosomal RNA (rRNA), and for the 9 cases, total RNA that includes rRNA was prepared.

claim: The log-fold change with rRNA and the adjusted log-fold change without rRNA are highly correlated (R2 ~0.99954).
source: As one can see in Figure 1, the log-fold change with rRNA and the adjusted log-fold change without rRNA are highly correlated (R2 ~0.99954).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1, which displays the correlation between the two measures.

claim: The nine BALF samples used in the analysis were taken from severely ill patients in Wuhan China in an attempt to identify the as-yet-unidentified pathogen causing their symptoms.
source: The nine BALF samples used in our analysis were taken from severely ill patients in Wuhan China in an attempt to identify the as-yet-unidentified pathogen causing their symptoms and were not prepared in conjunction with control samples.
evidence: The claim describes the origin and context of the COVID-19 case samples.

claim: The nine BALF samples were not prepared in conjunction with control samples.
source: The nine BALF samples used in our analysis were taken from severely ill patients in Wuhan China in an attempt to identify the as-yet-unidentified pathogen causing their symptoms and were not prepared in conjunction with control samples.

claim: The low read-depth of the nine BALF samples resulted in high false-positive (off-target) counts due to the presence of Alu elements in some of the transcripts.
source: The low read-depth of the nine BALF samples resulted in high false-positive (off-target) counts due to the presence of Alu elements in some of the transcripts, which can be seen in the read mapping files (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of read mapping files shown in Figure 2.

claim: The authors used highly stringent mapping parameters in CLC Genomics Workbench with 0.95 length and 0.95 similarity match to reduce off-target mapping.
source: Instead, to reduce off-target mapping, we used the much more conservative approach of 0.95 length and 0.95 similarity match.
evidence: The claim describes the specific parameters used in the authors' analysis.

claim: The default parameters for the CLC Genomics Workbench algorithm are to score a 'match' for a read if at least 0.80 of the fragment matches the gene and if the similarity is 0.8 or greater.
source: The default parameters for this algorithm are to score a "match" for a read if at least 0.80 of the fragment matches the gene and if the similarity is 0.8 or greater.
evidence: The claim describes the default settings of the software used.

claim: Given the highly stringent parameters and the much larger read depth of the control samples, any genes that are expressed in COVID-19 BALF samples but are not present in controls have a high probability of being true positives.
source: Given these highly stringent parameters, and the much larger read depth of the control samples, any genes that are expressed in COVID-19 BALF samples, but are not present in controls, have a high probability of being true positives and the fold-increase is likely an underestimate.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the analysis parameters and sample characteristics.

claim: Tissue factor (F3) contains an Alu element in the 3'UTR of the gene.
source: Indeed, not only does tissue factor (F3) contain an Alu element in the 3'UTR of the gene, the read mapping file in CLC Genomics Workbench clearly shows for both cases and controls, that the majority of the fragments map to multiple places in the transcriptome (yellow in Figure 2), and cannot be assigned to F3 with confidence.
evidence: The claim is supported by the genomic structure of F3 and visualization in Figure 2.

claim: The authors used the lowest number in the matrix of gene counts as the denominator to account for situations where the denominator of the controls was zero.

evidence: The claim describes a methodological approach used in the analysis.
